Collection without pagination or idempotency
An unpaginated collection degenerates: huge responses, timeouts, useless load, impossible to consume at large volumes. Without idempotency, a retry (network, client) duplicates business effects (payment, creation).

Big Ball of Mud — architecture without boundaries
The founding paper (Foote & Yoder, PLoP 1997) describes the BBoM as a "de facto" architecture: every local decision is fast, but the cost of maintenance and comprehension grows without bound, testability drops, and major refactors become impossible without a rewrite.

Bloater — overlong method/function, bloated data
"Bloaters" are the breeding ground of bugs: a long function makes error paths hard to audit, bloated data creates impossible states (incoherent field combinations), duplication makes fixes diverge. The refactoring catalog (Fowler) treats these smells by extraction.

Distributed monolith — services coupled at runtime
The distributed monolith combines the costs of a distributed system (latency, partial failures, deployments) with the drawbacks of a monolith (coupling, coordinated changes) — the worst of both worlds. It is the most frequent failure of microservices migrations.

God Object — central type that does everything
The god object violates cohesion: every modification touches a shared type, transitive dependencies multiply, unit testing becomes expensive (monster builder), and concurrency on the central state creates races.

Nano-services — decomposition too fine-grained
Fine-grained decomposition multiplies failure points, inter-service latency, and operation cost without bringing a business boundary: overall maintainability degrades while each unit is "clean". It is the inverse over-correction of the monolith.

Database shared between services
The shared database reintroduces the coupling decomposition was supposed to eliminate: services are bound by the schema, changes are coordinated, the database becomes the bottleneck and the single point of failure — it is the main symptom of the distributed monolith (see arch-distributed-monolith).

Stale cache — inconsistency with the source
A cache that drifts serves false facts (wrong prices, oversold stock); the cache consistency discipline (redis.io) is to bound this drift according to the business requirement. Uncontrolled drift erodes trust in the whole system.

Cache stampede — collapse of simultaneous accesses
The stampede (dog-piling) turns a banal expiration into an outage: the source receives n times the normal load at the worst moment. Without protection, the collapse repeats at every expiration cycle.

Configuration values hardcoded in the code
Hardcoded values violate configuration externalization (CWE-15, Twelve-Factor): change = redeployment, environments confused, secrets exposed (see sec-hardcoded-credentials) and risk of configuration drift between environments.

CLI that abuses flags and ignores conventions
CLI conventions are 40 years old: users and scripts expect them (help, `-h/--help`, `--version`, exit code 0/≠0, options on stdin when needed). Ignoring them makes the tool unpredictable, non-scriptable, and costly to adopt — the clig.dev guide documents these expectations.

Receiver closes the channel — double-close and send-on-closed panics
Channel close races are logic errors, not subtle race conditions: they exist because nobody agreed who owns the channel. The runtime panics on double close and on send after close, crashing the whole program.

Dynamic queries forced onto a static code generator
sqlc only generates STATIC queries: dynamic WHERE/ORDER BY are explicitly out of scope (issues #3414, #2061, discussion #364). Forcing dynamic behavior produces fragile, unreadable code — or worse, an unparameterized interpolation of SQL fragments that opens injection. It is the first adoption friction point of sqlc (top issues by reactions).

Entity-Attribute-Value (EAV) for structured data
EAV sacrifices schema guarantees: no type, no NOT NULL/CHECK constraint, no natural index, costly JOINs and pivots, integrity managed in the application. The complexity moves from the schema into every query.

Function applied to an indexed column in the WHERE clause
A function on the column makes the index unusable: the DBMS scans all rows and computes the function on each one. The cost goes from logarithmic to linear as soon as the table grows — it is the #1 cause of queries that "suddenly slow down".

N+1 query — one query per item
Each item costs a network round trip + execution plan: a list of 1000 items generates 1001 queries, seconds of latency and useless load on the database. It is the most cited SQL performance problem.

SQL injection via query modes and dollar-quoted literals
Parameterized queries protect values, not the SQL text: if the SQL itself contains uncontrolled fragments (`$tag$` literals, assembled clauses), an attacker can close the literal and inject commands. This bug class reappeared 3 times on pgx in 2 years (CVE-2024-27304, CVE-2026-33815/33816, GO-2026-5004).

Misconfigured connection pool (defaults or leaks)
`sql.Open` is lazy (no connection opened at call time) and the defaults are dangerous: unlimited pool, connections aging without `ConnMaxLifetime` (failures after failover/firewall), leaks from unclosed rows. The consequences (blocking, DB timeouts) only appear under load.

Raw BEGIN/COMMIT SQL instead of the transaction API
The official documentation says it: in concurrent programming, raw BEGIN/COMMIT can leave the database in an unpredictable state — the underlying connection can be reused by another goroutine between two Exec calls, and rollback is not guaranteed on error (locked connection, open transaction).

SELECT * in production — unnamed columns
`SELECT *` transfers all columns (including blob, large json, columns added later), prevents the optimizer from using covering indexes, and breaks `Scan` as soon as a column is added/removed — the contract becomes implicit and fragile.

Exported or string-typed context key
The official documentation is explicit: keys must be of a type defined in the caller's package and unexported. A string or exported key creates silent collisions between packages (two packages write the same key, reading a corrupted value) and makes the API impossible to inspect.

Ignored context or cancel never called
An accepted but unused context is a correctness bug, not a style issue: the caller that cancels or imposes a deadline is silently ignored — the code keeps running until the end of the operation. A `cancel` never called leaks one goroutine per operation (see go-goroutine-leak).

Comparing errors by string instead of errors.Is/As
Messages are display details, not a contract: they change, they are localized, and a message can be wrapped several times by `%w`. String comparison breaks on refactor and ignores the error chain (`errors.Is` traverses the `%w` wrappers).

Goroutine leak — goroutine launched without a guaranteed exit path
Each leak consumes a stack and its references; leaks accumulate silently until OOM. It is a permissive bug: no runtime warning, it only reveals itself in production.

Ignored error — return value discarded
Go treats errors as values; discarding them produces silent failures (truncated write, uncommitted transaction, under-billing) that only manifest later, with no link to the cause.

init() with side effects — implicit initialization
`init` execution is implicit, unordered (import order, undefined between files of the same package) and not directly testable: initialization failures are impossible to simulate, hidden dependencies complicate tests, and global state (see go-mutable-global-state) is shared.

Interface for every dependency (over-abstraction)
The interface adds indirection without benefit: costly navigation, more complex tests, and a larger API surface to maintain. The Go wiki recommends defining an interface where it is consumed, when an abstraction is really needed — not by default.

omitempty hiding significant zeros
The zero is silently omitted: the consumer can no longer distinguish "absent" from "zero" — counters shown as zero by default, conditions false by default, implicit API contracts that change on refactor. A field's semantics must not depend on the serialization tag.

Loop variable capture in a goroutine
Before Go 1.22, all iterations share the same variable: goroutines read the final value or a concurrent value — duplicated outputs, wrong data, data race.

Mutable state at package level (global variables)
Mutable globals create hidden dependencies: packages call each other implicitly, the initialization order (`init`) is opaque, tests are no longer isolated (non-determinism), and concurrency introduces races. It is the classic vector of "works in dev, not in prod" bugs.

Over-structuring — copy of golang-standards/project-layout
`golang-standards/project-layout` is not an official standard (Go team): the official module organization doc recommends staying simple and creating only the needed packages. Over-structuring increases the navigation cost, encourages catch-all packages, and dilutes responsibilities.

Panic/recover used as a general try/catch
An uncaught panic kills the process (or the goroutine, for HTTP handlers); a generic recover masks real bugs and loses the value and the stack trace. Control-flow-based error handling is unreadable and breaks `errors.Is/As`.

Reflection overuse — dynamic dispatch where concrete code suffices
Reflection moves type errors from compile time to runtime, is slow (allocations, dynamic dispatch), and defeats readability and compiler optimization. The official guide concludes: "It's a powerful tool that should be used with care and avoided unless strictly necessary."

Shadowing — variable masked by an inner declaration
Shadowing produces silent bugs: an assignment that "does not take", a masked `err` that does not propagate the error, a variable confusion that survives refactors. The compiler does not warn (legal in Go).

String concatenation in a loop with +=
Go strings are immutable: each `+=` copies the whole string. For n iterations, the cost is O(n²) with n allocations — visible from a few thousand iterations, catastrophic in a data pipeline.

HTTP server without timeouts (default values)
ServeMux defaults impose no timeouts: a slow client occupies a worker indefinitely, idle connections accumulate, and a blocked handler grows the queue — trivial denial of service (slowloris) and unavailability under load. The Cloudflare guide documents the distinction between server and handler timeouts.

Consumer offset commit misordering
Commit too early = message loss on failure; commit too late or out of order = reprocessing and duplicates. Both modes corrupt stream accuracy (at-most-once vs uncontrolled at-least-once).

Poison pill without a dead-letter queue (DLQ)
A poison pill halts the progress of the whole partition: the following (valid) messages are never processed, endless retries waste CPU, and processing order is lost. Automatic retry does not fix a structurally invalid message.

Retry storm — aggressive retries without a limit or breaker
The Microsoft architecture center documents the retry storm as a major cause of outages: synchronized retries (all clients retrying at the same time) turn a limited failure into a general collapse. Without a breaker, failure propagates instead of isolating.

Excessive logging — noise without signal
Noise is expensive (storage, I/O, CPU) and degrades debugging: the more you log, the less logs are read. Hot paths slow down under load, and high-cardinality logs break collection systems (indexing).

Logging mistaken for observability
Logging alone is passive: it records what you thought to log before the incident, with no structure to answer new questions. Observability links logs, metrics and traces (correlation) to reconstruct the behavior of a distributed system.

API that ignores HTTP semantics (statuses, cache, types)
Statuses and headers are the protocol contract: ignoring them breaks standard clients (caches, proxies, libs), hides real errors (4xx cannot be distinguished from 5xx), and forces every client to invent its own error detection.

RPC tunnel — everything through GET or POST
Reinventing RPC over HTTP loses the protocol's guarantees: caching, idempotency, standard statuses, discovery. Clients can infer nothing, the API is opaque, and destructive GETs cause accidents.

Cross-Site WebSocket Hijacking — missing origin validation
The browser does not apply the same-origin policy to WebSockets: it is up to the server to validate the Origin at the handshake (WSTG, CWE-1385). Without this validation, an attacker hijacks the established session (CSWSH) to read data, issue commands or exhaust connections — since the browser's origin IP is legitimate, network protections see nothing.

Internal information leak through errors
Error messages reveal the internal structure (DB schema, stack, paths, versions) and ease targeted attacks; distinguishing raw/internal vs external errors is a documented security control (OWASP error handling, A05 security misconfiguration).

Fail open — security disabled by default or on error
A fail-open turns an outage into a breach: the smallest error (IdP timeout, middleware bug, forgotten config) lets unauthenticated access through. Permissive defaults are the most dangerous error class because they stay silent until the incident.

Hardcoded secrets (passwords, keys, tokens)
A secret in code is exposed to anyone who reads the repository (internal, fork, CI logs, artifacts); CWE-15 classifies configuration externalization as a security control. Once leaked, the only response is secret rotation — costly and often forgotten.

Trusting the client IP from unverified proxy headers
A client can forge X-Forwarded-For (e.g. `X-Forwarded-For: 127.0.0.1`): only the segments appended by proxies you control are trustworthy (MDN). A forged IP bypasses per-IP rate limiting, falsifies audit, defeats geo-protections, and subverts decisions based on network identity — with no trace of intrusion.

Cookie sessions without CSRF protection
A third-party site can trigger cross-site requests that carry the session cookie (the browser sends it automatically): deletion, transfer, password change without the user's knowledge (CSRF attack, dedicated OWASP cheat sheet). SameSite=Strict mitigates but does not cover every context (subdomains, SameSite=Lax on GET).

No threat model — "safe" design by intuition
Design flaws (authorization by default, exposed objects, untrusted file handling) are not code bugs: scanners cannot detect them and they cost a rewrite once discovered. Without a threat model, security rests on intuition and forgetfulness.

SSH host key shared across instances or regenerated at every boot
A shared private key is "only as private as it is shared": compromising one instance allows impersonating all the others (undetectable MITM for clients that pinned this key). A key regenerated at every boot breaks pinning (TOFU) and opens the door to a fraudulent first contact; sshd also refuses key files accessible to group/world.

Timing-unsafe comparison — byte-by-byte equality of secrets
An early-exit comparison leaks how many leading bytes matched through timing; an attacker can recover the secret byte by byte. crypto/subtle exists exactly for this. Note that even ConstantTimeCompare leaks a length difference (golang/go#18936), so compare equal-length digests.

Unsanitized HTML rendering — markdown and templates on uncontrolled input
Rendering uncontrolled input as HTML without sanitization is an open XSS door: a user can inject script executed in other users' contexts (session, CSRF, exfiltration). Markdown parsers render raw HTML blocks by default — this is a format contract, not a parser bug.

Weak randomness — math/rand for security-sensitive values
math/rand output is predictable: the package docs state it "should not be used for security-sensitive work" and that its outputs "might be easily predictable regardless of how it's seeded". Predictable values defeat tokens, reset keys, and challenge-response flows.

Brittle tests — failures on legitimate refactors
A brittle test costs more than it brings: it blocks legitimate changes, teaches the team to ignore the suite (and therefore real regressions), and consumes team time. The test smells literature (xUnit Test Patterns) ranks brittleness among the worst test defects.

Testing the implementation, not the behavior
Implementation tests freeze details that must remain free to change: they turn every refactor into test work, inflate maintenance, and do not protect the real contract — the behavior observable from the outside.

Mocking everything — the fake becomes the system
Mocks only verify programmed expectations: they freeze the internal API (see test-implementation-details), detect neither real contract errors nor integration regressions, and give false confidence. The test hierarchy (pyramid) requires more real low-level tests than mocks.

Tests based on real time (sleep)
A sleep is an arbitrary delay: too short → flaky, too long → slow suite; it provides no synchronization guarantee. Time-based concurrency tests mask races instead of revealing them — `go test -race` is not enough if the assertion waits for nothing.

MCP server shape — primitives, transport, and trust boundary
Exposing capabilities to an LLM agent without a framework produces ad-hoc servers, blurry security boundaries, and protocols that are incompatible across clients (IDEs, agents, applications). How do you structure an MCP server coherently with the spec?

Modular monolith — strong internal boundaries
Premature microservice decomposition adds latency and operational cost without real business boundaries (see pattern:antipattern:arch-distributed-monolith); the spaghetti monolith, for its part, becomes unmanageable.

Ports & adapters — domain decoupled from infrastructure
Business logic mixed with infrastructure (HTTP, SQL, files) makes the domain impossible to test in isolation and coupled to every technology (see pattern:antipattern:arch-big-ball-of-mud).

Stale-while-revalidate — freshness without load spikes
Expiration of a popular entry causes a spike of simultaneous misses (stampede, see pattern:antipattern:cache-stampede) and blind invalidation serves stale data without control (see pattern:antipattern:cache-stale).

Structured CLI — subcommands and conventions
A CLI without structure (global flags, ad hoc actions, inconsistent output) is unpredictable and not scriptable (see pattern:antipattern:cli-flag-and-convention-abuse).

Channel ownership — one sender, sender closes
Sending on a closed channel panics, and so does closing a channel twice. Without an explicit owner, "who closes the channel" races between goroutines and fails only under load (see pattern:antipattern:concurrency-close-from-receiver).

Pipeline — goroutine stages connected by channels
Process a data stream in sequential stages (read → transform → write) while parallelizing each stage without goroutine leaks.

Singleflight — merge identical concurrent calls
N simultaneous requests miss a cache at the same instant and all hit the source (see pattern:antipattern:cache-stampede): multiplied load and latency spikes.

Worker pool — bounded fan-out with errgroup.SetLimit
Launching one goroutine per task without a limit exhausts memory and connections under load (see pattern:antipattern:go-goroutine-leak).

Externalized configuration — per-environment values
Per-environment values (URLs, ports, credentials) hardcoded in the source force a rebuild per environment and risk leakage (see pattern:antipattern:cfg-hardcoded-values).

Explicit and measured connection pool
Pool defaults (unlimited connections, never recycled, leaks) exhaust the DBMS or freeze the application under load (see pattern:antipattern:db-pool-misconfig).

Batch queries — eliminate the N+1 with JOIN/IN
One query per item (N+1) costs one round-trip per row and makes latency and load explode (see pattern:antipattern:db-n-plus-one).

Transaction boundary — BeginTx + deferred Rollback
Several writes must be atomic; a manual BEGIN/COMMIT or a commit without rollback leaves the database in an unpredictable state on error (see pattern:antipattern:db-raw-transactions).

Versioned migrations — the schema is code
Modifying the schema in production with ad hoc SQL or a hand-run "ALTER" makes the database state unknown and environments diverge.
Bootstrap CLI and canonical agent runtime

Concrete returns, consumer-side interfaces
A function that returns an interface forces all its callers into an abstraction, often for a single implementation — indirection without benefit (see pattern:antipattern:go-interface-everywhere).

Constructor injection — explicit dependencies without a framework
Dependencies (db, logger, config, clients) are read from globals or built inside the types: impossible to replace in tests, opaque initialization order, shared state (see pattern:antipattern:go-mutable-global-state).

Contextual worker — goroutine with an explicit exit condition
Starting a goroutine is trivial; stopping it cleanly is not. Without an exit condition, goroutines leak (memory, stack) until OOM.

Error chain — wrap with %w and inspect with errors.Is/As
An error propagated without context loses its origin: impossible to know which operation failed (which repository, which network call) once at the top of the stack.

Generics when they pay — write them for many types, not one call site
Generic code adds constraints, inference complexity, and compile cost; used speculatively it makes simple code harder to read and is a premature abstraction (see pattern:antipattern:go-interface-everywhere for the interface-side trap).

internal/ packages — hide API that is not for external consumers
Every exported package is a promise: consumers can import it, so changing it later breaks them. Helper and cross-cutting packages end up exported by default even when only the module itself uses them.

Minimal layout — packages by import boundary
The tree copied from a generic template (cmd/pkg/internal/scripts…) creates empty packages and artificial layers for a small project (see pattern:antipattern:go-over-structuring).

Private and typed context keys
Carry request values (user ID, request ID, tenant) in the context without collision or implementation leakage between packages.

Semantic import versioning — /vN module path for breaking changes
A breaking API change inside the same module path silently breaks consumers: one module path means one API, and the import path cannot express "this is v2" without the /vN convention.

Sentinel, typed, and opaque errors
Every caller must decide what to do based on an error's cause, but without a common strategy comparisons are fragile (strings) or couple the caller to the implementation.

String building — strings.Builder for loop assembly
Go string immutability makes loop concatenation quadratic (see pattern:antipattern:go-string-concat-loop): every `+=` copies the whole string.

Value vs pointer receivers — choose by mutation, size, and method set
The receiver kind is a contract: a value receiver copies the struct and cannot mutate it, a pointer receiver can mutate and adds the method to the method set of *T only. The wrong choice silently copies on every call, or excludes the type from interfaces it should satisfy.

Zero value usable — design types so the zero value is ready to use
A type whose zero value panics or misbehaves forces every user to remember an initialization ritual; the zero value becomes a trap instead of the default, and constructors proliferate to hide it.

Idempotency keys — safe retries for writes
A network or client retry duplicates a business effect (payment, creation, sending) — POSTs are not idempotent by nature (see pattern:antipattern:api-no-pagination).

Middleware chain — clean cross-cutting composition
Cross-cutting concerns (logging, auth, recovery, CORS, rate limiting) duplicated in every handler become inconsistent and easy to forget (see pattern:antipattern:rest-ignoring-http-semantics).

Cursor pagination — stable and bounded lists
An unpaginated collection degenerates into huge responses; offset pagination drifts when data changes between pages (see pattern:antipattern:api-no-pagination).

REST modeling — resources, verbs, and statuses
An API that tunnels everything through generic POST/GET is opaque: no caching, no idempotency, unusable statuses (see pattern:antipattern:rest-tunneling).

Dead-letter queue — isolate unprocessable messages
A structurally invalid message loops in retry and blocks the partition (see pattern:antipattern:msg-poison-pill-no-dlq): valid messages behind it are never processed.

Idempotent consumer — absorb duplicates
Queues guarantee at-least-once delivery: a message can be received several times (rebalance, retry, redelivery). Processing a non-idempotent effect twice produces duplicates (see pattern:antipattern:msg-offset-commit-misorder).

Transactional outbox — event and state atomic
Publishing an event and changing state cannot be atomic directly (dual-write): the event is lost if publication fails, or duplicated if the transaction is replayed.

Correlation identifiers — link a request's signals
In a distributed architecture, a user action crosses several services: without a common link, the logs of each step are islands and the incident is impossible to reconstruct (see pattern:antipattern:obs-logging-not-observability).

Structured logging — slog as the standard interface
Free-form text logs (fmt.Printf) are neither filterable, nor correlatable, nor queryable at scale — and noise destroys value (see pattern:antipattern:obs-excessive-logging).

Circuit breaker — fail fast to isolate a dependent
A failing dependent still receives every request despite its failures: callers wait for timeouts, threads/goroutines exhaust, and the failure propagates (see pattern:antipattern:msg-retry-storm).

Retry with exponential backoff and jitter
Transient errors (timeout, 5xx, connection) are frequent; without retry the system is fragile, with aggressive retry it collapses (see pattern:antipattern:msg-retry-storm).

Strict deadlines — context deadlines at every boundary
Without a deadline, a blocked call (network, DB, service) freezes a worker indefinitely and latency accumulates (see pattern:antipattern:http-no-timeouts).

Authentication mechanism choice — cookie sessions vs JWT vs OAuth2
The choice of the auth mechanism drives revocation, CSRF, mobility, and complexity. JWT is often chosen by reflex ("stateless") while cookie sessions are simpler and revocable for a classic web app; conversely, cookie sessions for a mobile API multiply the pitfalls (CORS, CSRF, fixation).

Fail closed — deny by default
Access controls whose default allows (or that fail open on error) turn an outage into a breach (see pattern:antipattern:sec-fail-open).

Secrets management — out of code, rotatable
Secrets in code or artifacts are exposed to anyone who reads the repository, and rotating them becomes impossible without redeployment (see pattern:antipattern:sec-hardcoded-credentials).

Black-box package tests — test through the exported API
Tests in the same package can reach unexported identifiers, so they tend to assert internals; when the internals change, the tests break even though the exported behavior is intact (see pattern:antipattern:test-implementation-details).

Role-based fakes over interaction mocks
Interaction mocks freeze the internal API, make tests fragile, and verify expectations rather than contracts (see pattern:antipattern:test-over-mocking).

httptest — test HTTP handlers and clients without a port
Testing HTTP code by opening a real port is slow, fragile in CI, and does not test the handler as a real client would.

Testable seams — separate logic from effects
Logic mixed with effects (terminal, clock, framework) is impossible to test without heavy harnesses, and the tests become fragile (see pattern:antipattern:test-sleep-based and pattern:antipattern:test-implementation-details).

Table-driven tests — cases in a table, assertions in a loop
One test per case duplicates the harness (call, assertion, setup); copied tests diverge and edge cases are forgotten.
